title: Why NVIDIA Wants TSMC 3nm at the Base of Its Next-Generation HBM
author: M
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

NVIDIA is reportedly pushing Samsung Semiconductor, SK hynix, and Micron Technology toward TSMC’s advanced 3nm process for the base dies in its next generation custom high bandwidth memory, known as NVHBM. The development highlights how AI computing is reshaping relationships between processor designers, memory manufacturers, and foundries.

The distinction matters: this does not mean the entire memory stack moves to 3nm. HBM combines stacked DRAM dies with a base die beneath them. The reported requirement concerns that logic layer, while the memory dies continue to use specialized DRAM manufacturing processes.

According to Seoul Economic Daily, NVIDIA wants a common manufacturing foundation across its three suppliers to improve consistency and reduce the effort required to validate different implementations. Samsung reportedly accepted the request, although the arrangement should be understood as reported industry information rather than a jointly announced production agreement.

The technical direction builds on an established trend. SK hynix previously announced that adopting TSMC’s advanced logic technology for HBM base dies would enable more functionality within limited space and support customization for performance and power efficiency.

For Samsung, the reported decision is particularly significant. Its integrated memory and foundry businesses have supported an internal manufacturing approach. Using TSMC for NVIDIA’s custom product would show how customer requirements can outweigh traditional competitive boundaries.

Strategically, a shared process could simplify NVIDIA’s supplier qualification and platform integration. That is an implication of the reported approach, however, rather than proof that different suppliers’ finished products become interchangeable.

TSMC would gain another role in the AI supply chain, extending beyond accelerator manufacturing into customized memory logic.

The broader message is clear: AI performance increasingly depends on coordinated development across compute, memory, and packaging. NVIDIA’s influence now reaches deep into its suppliers’ technology choices, while memory differentiation increasingly involves logic design alongside DRAM density and bandwidth.
